Abstract
The emergence of micro-computed tomography has significantly enhanced our ability to 
examine the morphology of porous materials and the dynamics of fluid flow within pore 
spaces. However, image-based analyses can be compromised by various artifacts, particu-
larly ring artifacts, which appear as concentric rings in the images. These artifacts can be 
misinterpreted as part of the pore space, artificially connecting pores and thus influenc-
ing numerical simulations. This study examines the influence of ring artifacts on pore 
network modeling (PNM), direct numerical simulation (DNS), and prominent numerical 
techniques, and presents a computing approach for their effective mitigation. For this pur-
pose, a dataset was compiled from the literature that includes the images of Fontainebleau, 
Boise, and Belgian sandstones. Data augmentation was implemented by extracting real ring 
patterns from Fontainebleau samples and superimposing them onto clean images of the 
sandstones. Two U-Net autoencoder architectures (base and Attention U-Net) were trained 
for a regression task aimed at removing ring artifacts while reconstructing the underly-
ing pore morphologies. The Attention U-Net outperformed the base model, achieving a 
mean squared error of 0.07 (calculated based on the grayscale values between 0 and 255). 
Visual evaluations confirmed the model’s effectiveness in artifact removal and pore mor-
phology reconstruction. The model was further tested on unseen pore-scale data containing 
real ring artifacts, which indicated a high performance in removing the artifacts. DNS and 
PNM were performed on both original (with real rings) and improved 3D samples ­(2003 
voxels) to assess the impact of artifact removal on transport properties. The results revealed 
that ring artifacts, identified as flow pathways, significantly influence the velocity profiles. 
While the presence of the artifact had a minimal effect on porosity (a 1.68% error) and the 
number of pores (1.45% error), it significantly increased the permeability by 34%.

1  Introduction
Advances in high-resolution X-ray imaging techniques, such as micro-computed tomogra-
phy (or micro-CT), have paved the path for unveiling the internal morphology of materials 
(Blunt et al. 2013; Cnudde and Boone 2013; Withers et al. 2021). While images are used 
to evaluate the internal state of biomaterials (Ritman 2004), they provide insights into the 
geometrical and topological properties of the pore space, the fluid flow behavior, and the 
reaction phenomenon in porous media studies (Mahdaviara et al. 2023b; Mostaghimi et al. 
2013; Vogel 2002). However, the quality of the images can significantly influence the accu-
racy of the resulting pore-scale interpretations—for instance, introducing errors in absolute 
permeability estimates ranging from 3.9 to 43% across different gas diffusion layer samples 
(Mahdaviara et al. 2023c). Artifacts—various unintended distortions in the images—are a 
well-known challenge hindering the reliability of the pore-scale findings. These artifacts 
can hinder the reliable identification of pores, obscure pore–grain boundaries, and either 
disrupt or falsely suggest connectivity between pores, thereby misleading interpretations 
of fluid flow and transport in porous media. Such inaccuracies can propagate through 
upscaling procedures, ultimately distorting field-scale predictions and resulting in a flawed 
understanding of reservoir properties. This, in turn, poses significant challenges for select-
ing appropriate production strategies and may compromise the effectiveness of reservoir 
management decisions.
Despite advances in high-quality scanners and improvements in the scanning setups 
(Barrett and Keat 2004), artifacts are often inevitable on pore-scale images, necessitat-
ing additional image processing to minimize their impact (Fan et al. 2019). These arti-
facts can be categorized based on their origins into: physics-based, object-based, and hard-
ware-based artifacts (Barrett and Keat 2004; Boas and Fleischmann 2012; Sureshbabu and 
Mawlawi 2005). Physics-based artifacts arise from the physical processes during CT data 
acquisition. The common examples are beam hardening (Hsieh et al. 2000; Van Gompel 
et al. 2011), partial volume effects (Glover and Pelc 1980; Heckel et al. 2013), and scatter 
artifacts. Beam hardening occurs due to preferential attenuation of low-energy photons by 
a dense material such as metal minerals in a rock sample, leading to dark streaks and cup-
ping effects (Jeong and Ra 2009; Park et al. 2017; Pauwels et al. 2013). The partial volume 
effect is observed when multiple materials are present in a voxel (e.g., parts of the pore and 
grain). This leads to an averaged CT number, resulting in blurred pore-grain interfaces and

undistinguishable micropores, which remains an area of ongoing investigation within the 
porous media research community (Bultreys et al. 2015a, b; Ebadi et al. 2022). Apart from 
these challenges, the movement of the core sample during imaging (object-based artifact) 
leads to misregistration of the acquired data and a blurred image of the pore space (Chen 
et al. 2004; Spin-Neto and Wenzel 2016).
Ring artifacts, the central focus of this study, are prevalent hardware-related issues that 
manifest as concentric rings or stripes of varying radii within the reconstructed images 
(Anas et al. 2010; Ketcham and Carlson 2001; Wei et al. 2013). They primarily stem from 
inconsistencies or failures in the detectors during the CT scanning process (Boas and Fleis-
chmann 2012; Šalplachta et al. 2021; Vo et al. 2018). While flat-field correction (FFC) can 
partially mitigate these inconsistencies by normalizing detector responses, residual errors 
often remain and contribute to artifact formation. Although they originate from the same 
fundamental source—detector element errors or calibration issues—ring artifacts are dis-
tinct from spiral artifacts, which are typically observed in helical CT scans. This distinction 
stems from the geometry of the scanning trajectory: Circular acquisition paths give rise to 
ring artifacts, while helical paths transform similar detector errors into spiral-shaped dis-
tortions (Boas and Fleischmann 2012; Kalender 2011).
These artifacts are particularly problematic as they can obscure or mimic true struc-
tural details, resulting in potential misinterpretations. In porous media studies, the rings 
may appear with pixel/voxel values close to the pore space, making their delineation from 
the pores impossible. Apart from an increased porosity, the rings can establish unreal flow 
pathways by linking the unconnected pores, implying extensive errors in direct numerical 
simulation (DNS) and pore network modeling (PNM) outcomes. Accordingly, it is impera-
tive to eliminate the rings before modeling conduction.
Several traditional techniques exist for ring artifact removal from micro-CT images, 
including average filtering (Cai 2004b), histogram matching (Rakwatin et  al. 2007), 
Fourier transformation (Münch et al. 2009; Sijbers and Postnov 2004), and polar trans-
formation (Chao and Kim 2019; Lyckegaard et al. 2011; Prell et al. 2009). Filtering and 
histogram methods work in real space to reduce ring visibility while preserving context. 
Transformation techniques convert the image into another domain to facilitate correction. 
However, these methods may fail to completely remove rings or may inadvertently intro-
duce new artifacts.
Soft computing techniques have emerged as alternatives to traditional methods for 
addressing these issues. In 2021, a hybrid ring artifact reduction algorithm was introduced 
that combined CNNs trained on databases containing artifact-free images along with those 
featuring ring artifacts or sinogram domain-corrected images. This method successfully 
reduced ring artifacts without causing structural distortions (Chang et al. 2020). Fu et al. 
(2023) developed a multistage correction process based on wavelet coefficients to address 
ring artifacts in CT images. Their model, trained on synthetic data from the Div2k dataset 
(Timofte et al. 2018), effectively reduced ring artifacts while preserving image quality. Shi 
et al. (2024) proposed a method based on implicit neural representation (INR) for remov-
ing ring artifacts from sinogram data. By correcting defective pixel responses, their model 
improved artifact detection by focusing on stripe features.
Beyond ring artifact removal, soft computing methods have also been employed to 
address other artifact types, such as beam hardening and metal-induced artifacts, under-
scoring their broad applicability and effectiveness in artifact correction across various 
imaging challenges. Kalare et al. (2022) tackled beam hardening artifact removal using a 
cascaded deep neural network (CDNN) on 200 CT images of diverse body tissues. Saba-
Sadiya et al. (2021) demonstrated the efficiency of unsupervised learning methods, such

Most of the aforementioned studies have employed various geometric and frequency-
domain transformations. Additionally, they have focused primarily on artifact removal 
from medical images. This highlights the need to evaluate these techniques for delineating 
and removing artifacts from pore-scale images of porous media without relying on coordi-
nate transformations.
The current study investigates the effectiveness of U-Net and Attention U-Net encoder-
decoder architectures for ring artifact removal from X-ray images of porous media. The 
motivation for utilizing autoencoder-decoder models is their architectural robustness and 
their ability to generate output images with the same dimensions as the input, eliminat-
ing the need for manual reshaping or upsampling (Madani and Vlajic 2018; Schmidhuber 
2015). These advantages make them particularly well-suited for a range of image-based 
porous media applications, including binarization, multi-mineral segmentation, skeletoni-
zation, and noise reduction (Ar Rushood et al. 2020; Mahdaviara et al. 2023a; Wang et al. 
2021). Moreover, the integration of an attention mechanism enhances performance by ena-
bling the model to focus selectively on relevant regions, particularly those affected by ring 
artifacts (Oktay et al. 2018).
A dataset of 1430 2D images, each with dimensions of 1024 × 1024 pixels, was con-
structed using literature-published 3D micro-CT images of Fontainebleau, Boise, and Bel-
gian sandstones (Bultreys and De Boever 2020; Garing et al. 2017), encompassing image 
slices with both real and synthetic ring artifacts. The synthetic artifacts were generated 
by manually extracting real ring patterns from Fontainebleau samples and superimposing 
them onto real artifact-free slices of Fontainebleau, Boise, and Belgian samples. (Artifact-
free slices refer to those in which ring patterns are not visually discernible.) The moti-
vation for extracting ring patterns directly from real images is to capture the true visual

The autoencoders were trained on this dataset. The trained models significantly

2  Data Curation
As mentioned above, the datasets used in this study comprise X-ray images from three 
distinct core samples, including Fontainebleau (Garing et al. 2017), Boise (Garing et al. 
2017), and Belgian (Bultreys and De Boever 2020) sandstones (Fig. 2a). The Fontaineb-
leau images were associated with diverse ring artifact shapes and intensities. This diversity 
enhances the robustness of the models by exposing them to diverse artifact characteristics. 
However, the number of slices affected by artifacts was relatively limited, and the rings 
occupied only a minor portion of each slice, posing challenges for their recognition by 
predictive models. A large dataset including various pore space morphologies from dif-
ferent rock samples was necessary to ensure the model generality. To achieve this, data

augmentation was carried out by artificially superimposing synthetic ring artifacts onto

It should be mentioned that although the artifact does not affect a large portion of the 
images, it can significantly impact the simulation results by creating artificial throats link-
ing the previously unconnected pores.
The following steps were undertaken for the data augmentation (Fig. 2).
2.1  Ring Mask Generation
Several Fontainebleau slices containing ring artifacts were manually cleaned by removing 
the rings. For this purpose, the Clone Stamp tool in Adobe Photoshop was employed to 
manually replace the affected pixel values with those of adjacent, artifact-free pixels. Sub-
sequently, Python v3.9 was utilized to subtract the pixel values in the original images (with 
artifacts) from their corresponding corrected images. This procedure yielded various ring 
masks with distinct patterns and intensities, in which the unaffected areas were labeled as 
zero, and the affected regions were highlighted by the subtraction results.
To increase the diversity and population of the masks, these masks were subjected to 
common augmentation techniques, including rotation, flipping, and resizing (see Fig. 2b).
2.2  Superimposing on Clean Slices
The generated masks were randomly applied to the clean images of Fontainebleau, Boise, 
and Belgian sandstones. To this end, the coordinates of the regions in the clean images 
corresponding to the nonzero pixels in the masks were identified, and the pixel values in 
these regions were replaced with the corresponding values from the masks. This process 
brought about an extensive dataset including 1430 2D images, each with dimensions of 
1024 × 1024, representing various sandstone types (see Fig. 2c).
More details of the data curation section are presented in the “Data Preparation” section 
in the appendix.
3  Methodology
3.1  Machine Learning Modeling
As previously discussed, two autoencoder-decoders, U-Net and Attention U-Net, were 
employed for the aim of this study. Autoencoder-decoders, or simply autoencoders are a 
class of deep learning techniques widely used for image segmentation (Mahdaviara et al. 
2022; Siavashi et al. 2024), feature extraction (Mahdaviara et al. 2023b; Meng et al. 2017), 
dimensionality reduction (Wang et al. 2014, 2016), and data compression (Cheng et al. 
2018; La Grassa et  al. 2022). As illustrated in Fig.  3, their architecture comprises two 
blocks: an encoder and a decoder.
The encoder block is a set of convolutional and Maxpooling layers that transform the 
input data into a low-dimensional bottleneck space. The convolutional layers are the core 
component of the convolutional neural networks (CNNs), responsible for extracting the 
features from the input data by sliding one or more filters (or so-called kernels) with prede-
fined dimensions on the input (O’Shea 2015). Pooling layers serve as another crucial ele-
ment of CNNs, tasked with downsampling the feature maps generated by the convolutional

layers. Like convolution layers, they slide a filter on the image with a certain stride, which 
determines the filter movement size at each step (Gholamalinezhad and Khosravi 2020). 
In Maxpooling layers, the filter retains pixels with maximum value at each position, effec-
tively capturing the most significant features while discarding the rest. The input data are 
encoded by a set of convolutional and Maxpooling layers. Subsequently, a decoder block 
brings the encoded data back into the original dimension. For this, the decoder employs a 
set of convolutional and upsampling layers.
The generated image in the above-described forward pass is compared with the ground 
truth data using a loss function. Subsequently, the contribution of each parameter (filter 
weights) to the calculated loss is determined by computing the gradients through the back-
propagation process. These gradients are used by an optimization algorithm, to adjust the 
weights in the next iterations.
Several architectures of autoencoders, including U-Net (Ronneberger et al. 2015) and 
Attention U-Net (Oktay et al. 2018), have been introduced to enhance the performance of 
the network. U-Net is a well-known autoencoder that uses a skip connection from the cor-
responding layers in the encoder and decoder (with the same dimensions) to preserve the 
fine-grained features from upper levels that may be lost during the downsampling process. 
In Attention U-Net, an attention gate is added to improve performance, prioritizing the 
most significant features and filtering out irrelevant information. In this block, the feature 
map from the skip connection is multiplied by a trained weight, which is computed by the 
feature map from the skip connection with the upsampled feature map from a lower level 
of the decoder.
A description of the architecture of U-Net and Attention U-Net algorithms used in this 
study is presented in Table 2. To facilitate comparison, the same structure was utilized for 
both the U-Net and Attention U-Net. The encoder and decoder in each algorithm included 
4 levels with varying filter numbers ranging from 64 to 1024. The final layer incorporated a 
“Softmax” activation function.
3.2  Fluid Flow Modeling
Fluid flow simulations using DNS and PNM were performed on both the original and cor-
rected 3D Fontainebleau sandstone samples ­(2003 voxels). For DNS, the volume-averaged 
form of the Stokes equation was numerically solved (Whitaker 2013). Periodic boundary 
conditions were applied, while no-slip conditions were enforced at the fluid-grain interface. 
The system of equations was solved using the finite volume method, with the discretization 
performed on a staggered grid (Harlow and Welch 1965). For PNM, the skeleton and dis-
tance map of the images were extracted to construct the pore network. Skeletonization was 
performed using a thinning technique to identify the locations of pores and throats, as well 
as their interconnections. The distance map, which calculates the Euclidean distance of 
each voxel from its nearest boundary, was used to determine the pore and throat diameters. 
The simulations were performed using pore network model PoreFlow (Raoof et al. 2013).

4  Results and Discussion
As stated above, this study aims to investigate the impact of ring artifacts on image-based 
characterization of porous media. A primary objective is to train an AI algorithm to effec-
tively mitigate these artifacts, thereby enhancing the accuracy of subsequent PNM and 
DNS analyses. For this purpose, two autoencodes (base and Attention U-Net) were trained 
based on the image data of three sandstones described in the “Data Curation” section. 
A comparison between the performances of the models (see Fig. 4) indicates the effec-
tiveness of both algorithms for artifact removal, achieving the final test MSE values of 
0.076 and 0.070, respectively. However, incorporating Attention mechanisms marginally 
improves the accuracy of the artifact removal, and reduces the number of required epochs 
from 90 to 50 (see Fig. 4a, b). Moreover, the initial MSE of U-Net (in the primary epoch) 
is around 10 for both training and test loss. In contrast, in Attention U-Net, this number is 
reduced to 1.58 (1.66 for training), demonstrating a more rapid convergence during train-
ing. A more subtle yet important difference lies in the gap between the training and test 
loss as training progresses. As shown in Fig. 4a, the gap between these curves increases 
for the base U-Net, demonstrating its greater propensity for overfitting. This phenomenon 
occurs when a model becomes completely reliant on the training data, thereby compromis-
ing its generalization on unseen data (Anas et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2004). According to 
these discussions, the Attention U-Net model indicates superior performance in recogniz-
ing and removing ring artifacts.

To explore how removing ring artifacts influences simulation results, fluid flow simulations 
were conducted using the DNS and PNM techniques on both the original and corrected 3D 
samples of Fontainebleau sandstone, with dimensions of ­2003 voxels (see Fig. 13 in Appen-
dix for a schematic of the sample; for details of the fluid flow modeling refer to the Method-
ology section). The pore network, pressure distribution, and flow profile obtained via PNM, 
alongside the pressure and velocity profiles derived from DNS, are presented in Fig. 7 for the 
original (Fig. 7a) and corrected images (Fig. 7b). Figure 7a illustrates how the ring artifact in 
the original image introduces artificial flow pathways, which is shown by red within the pore 
network plot. These pathways result in an artificially increased flow velocity, evident in both 
the DNS velocity and PNM velocity profiles shown in Fig. 7a, b. The DNS-calculated aver-
age velocity per slice for the original image exceeds that of the corrected image in the x- and 
y-flow directions across all slices (see Fig. 7c, d). The most significant difference occurs in the 
x-direction at slice 100, where the artifact is present (Fig. 7c). In contrast, the artifact has mini-
mal impact on the flow velocity in the z-direction as it is oriented perpendicular to the artifact 
Fig. 7e.
Furthermore, the average pressure per slice in all directions is lower in the original image, 
suggesting that the ring artifact artificially facilitated fluid flow across the sample (see 
Fig. 7f–h). While the ring artifacts caused a relatively small error in total porosity (1.68%) 
(Fig. 7j), their impact on permeability was substantial, with errors of 34%, 20.3%, and 1.1% in 
the x-, y-, and z-directions, respectively (Fig. 7i). This difference shows the extent to which the 
artifact created false fluid pathways by connecting isolated pores.
Additional evidence of the artifact’s impact is provided by the reduction in average coordi-
nation number from 2.23 to 2.16 (Fig. 7l), the decrease in the total number of pores from 840 
to 828, and the reduction in the number of throats from 937 to 896 (Fig. 7k) after correction. 
The results indicate that the Attention U-Net algorithm successfully removed the misleading 
artificial pathways.
Overall, the findings of this study reveal the high performance of deep learning techniques 
in recognizing and removing ring artifacts, thereby improving the accuracy of pore space 
characterization and fluid flow modeling. Although efforts were made to enhance the mod-
el’s generalizability by providing synthetic data closely resembling real data, there remains 
room for improvement. Specifically, generating a larger dataset of real artifact-affected images 
from various porous media types could further refine the model. Additionally, future research 
should explore the application of AI in addressing other common artifacts, such as partial vol-
ume effects, which are frequently encountered in digital rock physics (DRP) studies.

Appendix A
Data Preparation
To train a supervised machine learning model, it is necessary to prepare two distinct data-
sets: one for inputs and one for outputs. This allows the model to compare its predicted 
results against known outputs and calculate the error, which is then used to improve its per-
formance. In this study, the input images are either of low quality or contain artifacts, while 
the corresponding outputs are high-quality, artifact-free images.
As previously mentioned, although some of the available images contain real ring arti-
facts, their quantity is insufficient for effective model training. Therefore, data augmenta-
tion is required. Additionally, to create accurate ground truth images, any naturally occur-
ring artifacts must be removed. The data preparation process involves the following four 
steps, which are illustrated in Fig. 8.
Real Artifact Removal
Naturally occurring ring artifacts must be removed to create clean ground truth images. 
Given the limited number of such images, a manual correction approach is employed using

the stamp tool in Photoshop software to eliminate visible ring artifacts. This results in a 
clean dataset suitable for use as ground truth.
Real Artifact Extraction
The underlying assumption is that artifacts are extraneous additions to an image. 
Therefore, if an artifact can be added, it can theoretically be isolated by subtracting it. 
After manually removing artifacts from the original images, the difference between the 
original (with artifacts) and the corrected (artifact-free) image reveals the ring artifact 
pattern. This subtraction technique allows for the extraction of artifact outlines. Image

Artificial Artifact Generation
The number of extracted ring artifacts is insufficient to capture the variability needed 
for robust training. To address this, data augmentation techniques are applied to the 
extracted artifacts. These include resizing, flipping, and rotating the artifact patterns to 
increase diversity in the training dataset.
Generation of Artificial Low‑Quality Images
The augmented artifact patterns are applied to clean, high-quality images to simulate 
ring artifacts. This is done by overlaying the artifact onto the image as a stencil. The 
intensity and scale of the applied artifacts can be fine-tuned using programming tools 
such as Python. This process results in a set of synthetic, artifact-degraded images to be 
used as inputs during training.

Abstract: The emergence of micro-computed tomography has significantly enhanced our ability to examine the morphology of porous materials and the dynamics of fluid flow within pore spaces. However, image-based analyses can be compromised by various artifacts, particu- larly ring artifacts, which appear as concentric rings in the images. These artifacts can be misinterpreted as part of the pore space, artificially connecting pores and thus influenc- ing numerical simulations. This study examines the influence of ring artifacts on pore network modeling (PNM), direct numerical simulation (DNS), and prominent numerical techniques, and presents a computing approach for their effective mitigation. For this pur- pose, a dataset was compiled from the literature that includes the images of Fontainebleau, Boise, and Belgian sandstones. Data augmentation was implemented by extracting real ring patterns from Fontainebleau samples and superimposing them onto clean images of the sandstones. Two U-Net autoencoder architectures (base and Attention U-Net) were trained for a regression task aimed at removing ring artifacts while reconstructing the underly- ing pore morphologies. The Attention U-Net outperformed the base model, achieving a mean squared error of 0.07 (calculated based on the grayscale values between 0 and 255). Visual evaluations confirmed the model’s effectiveness in artifact removal and pore mor- phology reconstruction. The model was further tested on unseen pore-scale data containing real ring artifacts, which indicated a high performance in removing the artifacts. DNS and PNM were performed on both original (with real rings) and improved 3D samples ­(2003 voxels) to assess the impact of artifact removal on transport properties. The results revealed that ring artifacts, identified as flow pathways, significantly influence the velocity profiles. While the presence of the artifact had a minimal effect on porosity (a 1.68% error) and the number of pores (1.45% error), it significantly increased the permeability by 34%. * Amir Raoof a.raoof@uu.nl * Mohammad Sharifi m_sharifi@aut.ac.ir
